external_sources.title: Childline: Asking an adult for help
external_sources.supports: Choose a trusted adult, plan a message, use speech or a note, and seek another adult if needed. Adults may need to share a safety concern with people who can help.

external_sources.title: PSHE Association: Handling complex issues safely
external_sources.supports: Use ground rules, distanced examples, a right to pass and appropriate safeguarding responses.

cases.text: Kit cannot read the first task instruction.
cases.next_step: Point to it and ask the adult to show the first step.
cases.staff_note: A short agreed wait can suit an ordinary task.

cases.text: Jo needs a private talk but finds speaking hard.
cases.next_step: Write or point to a private-talk request.
cases.staff_note: Use usual AAC and record the mode.

cases.text: The adult says later but gives no time or step.
cases.next_step: Ask when and what will happen next.
cases.staff_note: Do not accept a vague reply as a completed support plan.

cases.text: A person sends repeated messages that make Sam feel unsafe.
cases.fact: The messages cause a safety concern.
cases.next_step: Tell a trusted adult promptly and privately.
cases.staff_note: Do not show or collect real messages as class evidence.

cases.text: The first adult is away and Lee still needs help.
cases.staff_note: Staff confirm the available route before teaching.

cases.text: An adult ignores Rae’s concern about being hurt.
cases.fact: The safety concern has not been addressed.
cases.next_step: Tell another trusted adult and say help is still needed.
cases.staff_note: Never blame the learner for an adult’s poor response; follow safeguarding procedures.

PSHE-GROW-A2-W06 · Monday 7–Friday 11 December 2026
We Do: 5 minutes.
Teacher: Read the hinge aloud, ask for a choice and a reason. B. Ask for a clear next step or time. A hides the unmet need; C shares private information too widely. If the case is a safety concern, seek help promptly; immediate danger needs emergency help, not a delayed appointment. Reteach with “Please show me what to do next.”

Purpose and success checks
How can I make a clear request and check the reply?
I can choose who, how and when to ask. I can practise a clear help request. I can check the reply or use a backup.

Access and practice
Supported: point to a help phrase. Independent: choose who, how and when. Aspire: check a vague reply or a delay.
Model a vague reply with case A, then a helpful clarification. Each pupil makes a request and receives a real classroom reply. The adult records the response without supplying the learner’s reason.

Begin evidence during practice and finish during capture. Accept speech, pointing, drawing, writing or usual AAC. Scribe exact words without supplying the assessed reason. No forced pair work or public performance.
Safe teaching evidence and learner voice
Boundaries
Fictional cases only in group discussion. No acted threats, disclosure demand or live emergency call. Keep any real concern in the separate safeguarding process.
Assessment and feedback

Record the learner’s own words or signs, the adult’s real practice reply and a workable next step. Ordinary task help may wait for an agreed time; a safety concern needs prompt support. A scripted example is not evidence that an actual safeguarding event occurred.

Retain actual work, response mode and support. Use VF · WS · I · NS+ (Yellow Box) · // (self-edit) · ? (read back) · R (responded) · E (evidence in the school's evidence record). R requires Voice, Audience, an NS+ prompt and the learner’s response in their own colour. Record E only after evidence is banked. Blank forms and adult models are not completed learner evidence.
Lundy moments
Space: calm, accessible participation. Voice: a choice, reason or help request. Audience: the adult listens or reads and replies. Influence: record the support or next-step change made in response.
Speaking listening and writing
Make a request, listen, ask a clarifying question and record a next step. The receiving teacher maps authentic responses to their own portfolio; no communication criteria are assigned here.

Staff answers and response guide
Help that gets heard
These are possible responses and task guides, not learner observations. Accept a defensible answer based on the facts or actual work. Record each learner’s reasoning and support.

Model and hinge

Kit cannot read a task instruction. Kit points to the line and asks for help. The adult says they will help soon. Kit asks: When can we do the first step? The adult gives a clear time and step. Kit checks the step or asks another adult.

Individual evidence key

Record the learner’s own words or signs, the adult’s real practice reply and a workable next step. Ordinary task help may wait for an agreed time; a safety concern needs prompt support. A scripted example is not evidence that an actual safeguarding event occurred.
Feedback boundaries and next teaching
Card A: A short agreed wait can suit an ordinary task.
Card B: Use usual AAC and record the mode.
Card C: Do not accept a vague reply as a completed support plan.
Card D: Do not show or collect real messages as class evidence.
Card E: Staff confirm the available route before teaching.
Card F: Never blame the learner for an adult’s poor response; follow safeguarding procedures.
Common misunderstandings
A reply is not always a clear plan. Asking again or using another adult is allowed. A learner may communicate by pointing, note or AAC without speaking publicly.
Teaching boundary
Fictional cases only in group discussion. No acted threats, disclosure demand or live emergency call. Keep any real concern in the separate safeguarding process.
Feedback

If a reason is missing, return to the fact or actual work. Re-model a different example, then keep the learner’s own revision. Use NS+ and the learner response in their own colour before R. E means evidence actually banked. Keep safeguarding records separate.
